drills.q: maxEventTimeSeen is 09:47 and your watermark is withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes"). What is the current watermark, and what happens to a record with event_time = 09:29 arriving now?
drills.a: Watermark = 09:47 - 15min = 09:32. The record at 09:29 is older than the watermark, so it is dropped as too late rather than being merged into its window.

drills.q: A query does .groupBy(window("event_time","10 minutes")).count() with outputMode("complete"). Is this valid? What if it were a stream-stream join instead?
drills.a: Valid for the windowed aggregation — complete mode is supported for aggregations, re-emitting the whole result table each trigger. Not valid for a stream-stream join — joins only support append output mode, since a join's output rows are matched pairs with no defined 'this row changed' semantic; Spark rejects update/complete on a join at query-plan analysis time.

drills.q: Compute the state multiplier for window("event_time", "30 minutes", "10 minutes") versus an equivalent 30-minute tumbling window, and state when that extra cost is actually justified.
drills.a: Multiplier = window_size/slide_interval = 30/10 = 3x state versus tumbling. Justified when the business need is a genuinely frequently-refreshed rolling metric (e.g. a live dashboard needing an updated rolling 30-minute count every 10 minutes); not justified if consumers only read the value once per 30-minute boundary, where a tumbling window delivers equivalent information at a third of the state cost.

drills.q: Your Delta sink shows duplicate rows after a job restart even though you're using foreachBatch. Walk through what's missing and how txnAppId/txnVersion fixes it.
drills.a: Without idempotency tracking, a batch retried after a restart (because the sink write succeeded but the checkpoint commit hadn't landed yet, or vice versa) re-executes foreachBatch and writes the same rows again with no mechanism to recognize this as a repeat. Delta's txnAppId (a stable identifier for this pipeline) plus txnVersion (set to the Spark batchId) lets Delta's transaction log recognize 'this app already committed this version' and silently no-op a retried write with the same txnAppId/txnVersion pair, making the write idempotent per batch.

drills.q: A stream-stream join has a watermark on the left stream but not the right stream. What breaks, mechanically?
drills.a: The join buffer holding unmatched rows from the right stream has no bound on how long it waits for a matching left-side row, since there's no watermark on that side to declare rows 'too old to ever match.' The left side's buffer is bounded, but the right side's grows unboundedly for any right-side row that never finds a match, which is a real state-explosion cause — both sides of a stream-stream join need a watermark for the join's state to be bounded.

drills.q: Explain precisely why enabling Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) does not make your Structured Streaming-to-Kafka pipeline exactly-once end to end.
drills.a: Idempotent producer semantics operate at the scope of a single producer session's retries — they prevent a network-level retry of the same in-flight message from producing a duplicate. They have no visibility into or memory of a Spark micro-batch as a unit; if the whole batch is retried after a Spark restart (a new producer session attempts to resend rows the previous attempt already sent), idempotence within the new session does nothing to detect that the previous session already delivered those messages. The unit of duplication (a whole retried micro-batch after restart) is a different scope than the unit idempotence protects (a single message retry within one session).

drills.q: State size for a job has been growing steadily for a week with no watermark declared. You add a correctly-sized watermark today. Will state size immediately drop? Why or why not?
drills.a: Not immediately for all existing state — windows already open and older than the new watermark's cutoff will close and drop on the next trigger once the watermark logic evaluates them, but very recent/still-legitimately-open windows remain live as expected. Practically, most of the week's accumulated backlog of long-stale windows should clear within the first few triggers after the watermark is added, but genuinely recent, still-open windows continue to hold state exactly as the watermark design intends — the fix stops further unbounded growth immediately, and clears the specific stale backlog over the first several triggers rather than instantaneously.

drills.q: You must run an otherwise-continuous stateful streaming aggregation only once per hour via Airflow, catching up on however much backlog has accumulated since the last run. Which trigger do you use, and what do you still need to configure correctly for correctness?
drills.a: Trigger.AvailableNow(), which drains the available backlog across multiple appropriately-sized batches (respecting rate limits like maxOffsetsPerTrigger) instead of forcing everything through one oversized batch the way the deprecated Trigger.Once() would. You still need the watermark sized correctly for the aggregation's real lateness tolerance — trigger type is orthogonal to watermark/state semantics, and a stateful query run via AvailableNow still needs its state bounded exactly as it would running continuously.

drills.q: A colleague says 'we don't need to worry about exactly-once, Structured Streaming handles it.' Give the precise correction, referencing what the engine actually guarantees versus what the sink must provide.
drills.a: The engine guarantees exactly-once processing: offsets and operator state are committed atomically per batch via the checkpoint, so a restart never reprocesses a committed batch or skips an uncommitted one. It does not guarantee the sink write is exactly-once, because the sink write and the checkpoint commit are separate steps; a crash between them can duplicate output. Whether the pipeline is truly exactly-once end to end depends on whether the specific sink in use is idempotent (e.g. keyed upsert) or transactional (e.g. Delta txnAppId/txnVersion, or custom Kafka transactional foreachBatch logic) — 'Structured Streaming handles it' is only true once you've verified which mechanism the sink provides.

drills.q: Design a dead-letter strategy for records dropped by a watermark that's tuned tightly for latency reasons, where occasional data loss is unacceptable but low latency for the common case is required.
drills.a: Keep the tight watermark on the primary aggregation path for latency. Separately, run a parallel branch (or a second read of the same source) with no watermark, or a much looser one, that filters specifically for records whose event-time falls before the primary watermark's cutoff, and routes those to a dead-letter sink (a separate table or topic) for reprocessing or reconciliation. This way the low-latency path stays fast and bounded, while genuinely late records are captured rather than silently discarded, at the cost of a second read/processing path and a reconciliation step to merge dead-letter records back into the final dataset later.
